name: Eyelash curler
lead: An eyelash curler is a hand-held clamp with a curved frame and a replaceable rubber or silicone pad that bends the upper lashes into a curl. Users apply it at the lash base to make the eyes look larger and more open, often before mascara. Heated versions, introduced in the 1990s, are used to help the curl last longer. [1]

Published literature on the tool is largely injury and allergy case reports, plus one laboratory study that found lash curler use did not measurably change eyelash structure, unlike mascara frequency. [2][3][4][5][6]
infobox: Patent filed c. 1923, granted 1925 (US 1,542,014), per Grokipedia

paras: Standard curlers have two hinged handles, a curved upper bar, and a pad that cushions the lashes. Mini versions exist for the lash corners and for small eyes, and heated curlers use a battery-powered element. [1]

According to Grokipedia, the first verifiable patent was granted to Charles W. Stickel of Rochester, New York, in 1925, and the device was marketed as Kurlash. Later patents refined the clamp and pad. Heated curlers followed in the late 1990s, and Japanese manufacturers have been influential in curler design. [1] These details come from an AI-generated source and have not been independently verified here.
The clamp bends lashes around the curve of the pad and the shape holds because keratin partly sets in the new position; heat is claimed to extend it. [1]
Users and makeup guides describe a curled lash line as making eyes look wider. The curl is temporary and fades within hours. No trials of appearance effects were identified. [1]

A 2014 study using synchrotron X-ray tomography on lashes from 36 Japanese women found that mascara use frequency correlated with cuticle cracking and cortex porosity, while eyelash curler use did not alter lash structure to a statistically significant degree. [4]

Case reports describe nickel-related contact dermatitis from metal curlers, reported in 1985 and 1991. [5][6][7] Open-globe eye injuries involving curlers have also been reported, including a 2009 case report and a 2025 report in a beautician. [2][3] Optometry commentary lists curlers among cosmetic eye tools that can cause injury. [8]
Clinicians' general cautions, as reported in these sources, include avoiding pinching the lid, avoiding use with wet or heavily coated mascara that may pull lashes, and using heated tools carefully.

Lash curling is discussed as a quick, cheap way to open the eye area, and the site rates it as strong but temporary. Home lash-lift kits are discussed by consumers as a longer-lasting alternative. [9]

No trials of eyelash curlers for appearance were found. Human studies are limited to case reports of dermatitis and eye injury and one cross-sectional laboratory study of lash structure. [2][3][4][5][6][7]

timeline.event: US patent 1,542,014 granted to Charles W. Stickel for an eyelash crimping tool, per Grokipedia. [1]
Case reports of nickel dermatitis from eyelash curlers published. [5][6]
US patent for a heated curler granted, per Grokipedia. [1]
Study finds curler use did not significantly change lash structure. [4]

lore.intro: Eyelash curlers are discussed on looksmax.org mainly by male users asking whether curling natural lashes can improve the appearance of the eye area, and whether the tool damages lashes [10][11].

claims.claim: Curling lashes gives a 'prettyboy' effect and can disguise a weak eye area
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user with long natural lashes says curling them with his fingers hides part of his upper eyelid exposure (UEE) and gives a 'prettyboy' effect, and asks where to buy a curler [10].
claims.experts: No published studies in the sources reviewed here have examined whether lash curling changes perceived attractiveness or eye-area proportions; the clinical literature on curlers consists of injury and allergy case reports [2][3][5][6][7].

claims.claim: Curlers can cut or damage lashes, so finger-curling with Aquaphor is a better method
claims.believers: One reply in the thread says curlers can damage lashes and that he instead curls with his fingers after applying Aquaphor, though the curl lasts about two hours and needs repeating [10]. The original poster also asks whether curlers can cut lashes, citing complaints by TikTok users [10].
claims.experts: A synchrotron imaging study of lashes from 36 Japanese women found that mascara use frequency correlated with cuticle cracking and porosity; it did not test curlers [4]. No published studies in the sources reviewed here have compared finger-curling or Aquaphor with curlers.

claims.claim: A pricier, better-designed curler works better than a cheap one
claims.believers: Thread participants note curlers cost 2-3 euros in many shops but around 30 euros at beauty retailers, and one asks whether more expensive models are better [10]. A second thread's author says one specific brand is 'the one to go for' [11].
claims.experts: No published comparisons of curler brands, price tiers or pad designs were found in the sources reviewed here.

claims.claim: Curler use can be subtle enough that new acquaintances cannot tell, and is considered attractive
claims.believers: The author of a looksmax.org thread on 'eyelash curler maxxing' says that if used carefully, anyone who has not met him before probably would not be able to tell, and cites before-and-after images as examples of a look considered attractive [11].
claims.experts: No published research in the sources reviewed here evaluates how observers perceive men's curled lashes. A 2025 optometry clinical report on cosmetic eye enhancements discusses the eye-health caveats of such products [8].

claims.claim: Curlers are safe as long as the user is careful not to overdo it
claims.believers: The same author says he will 'have to be careful not to overdo it' and does not describe injury as a concern [11].
claims.experts: Case reports describe an open globe injury from an eyelash curler [2][3], and contact dermatitis from nickel in curlers [5][6][7]. Optometry commentary lists curler-related eye injuries among the risks of cosmetic eye enhancements [8].
